facts: The accused told the complainant that he could get her son a clerk's job in the railways through his contacts. He took four lakh rupees from her in cash, later handed over an appointment letter bearing a forged railway seal, and stopped answering her calls when her son reported for duty and was turned away.

charges.title: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property
charges.reason: The accused dishonestly induced the complainant to deliver property by falsely representing he could secure a railway clerk's job and subsequently absconded with the money.

charges.title: Forgery for purpose of cheating
charges.reason: The accused forged an appointment letter bearing a railway seal for the specific purpose of cheating the complainant out of her property.

charges.title: Punishment for cheating
charges.reason: By making false representations about his contacts and job placement, the accused deceived the complainant into handing over four lakh rupees.

sections.title: Cheating and dishonestly inducing delivery of property

defenses.argument: The prosecution has failed to prove that the accused 'dishonestly induced' the complainant to deliver property, as there is no evidence establishing a false representation of fact or a fabrication of facts. The accused merely made a promise based on his own unverified claim of having contacts; he did not actively fabricate a specific document or identity to deceive her into handing over the money. Without proof that the appointment letter was forged (which falls under IPC 468) or that the railway seal was actually forged, the element of dishonest inducement required for IPC 420 is missing.
defenses.fact_quote: He took four lakh rupees from her in cash, later handed over an appointment letter bearing a forged railway seal

defenses.argument: The charge of forgery for the purpose of cheating cannot be sustained because the prosecution has not adduced any evidence that the appointment letter or the railway seal was actually forged. The facts state only that the accused 'handed over an appointment letter bearing a forged railway seal,' but this is an assertion without corroboration. In the absence of proof that the document was a forgery, the essential ingredient of IPC 468—that the accused committed forgery intending it to be used for cheating—is not established.

defenses.argument: The prosecution has failed to prove that the accused 'cheated' in the sense of inducing delivery of property through deception, as the complainant voluntarily handed over cash based on a verbal promise rather than being induced by a fabricated fact or document. The subsequent failure to deliver the job and the non-appearance of the son do not constitute cheating under IPC 417; they are merely breaches of contract or promises. Mere delay or termination of an agency, without proof of active deception regarding facts, does not amount to cheating.

facts_profile.why: The facts disclose the offence of cheating by dishonestly inducing delivery of property through false representation and subsequent concealment of truth.
